It's actually a very common argument tactic used by people not arguing in good faith. It goes something like this:

"HAES is great."

"Actually there is no HAES and here are some studies linking obesity to every health problem."

"So what? HAES is about treating all people with love and respect and not judging them or discriminating against them."

At this point, the argument is no longer about reality and whether there is HAES. They have reframed it to be about feelings and attitudes instead of heath at every size. You have the choice of saying that "we should treat people with respect, but ... " at which point you have made a concession and they will treat it as a victory and an admission that they have the high ground; or you can argue we should not respect fat people, which is shaky because it's socially unacceptable and difficult to prove objectively.

Alternatively, you can attempt to bring the debate back with something like, "Do you deny that obesity is strongly linked to several health complications?" but it's so easy for them to ignore the question and bring it back to "it doesn't matter because they are people too." Most of the time you will find yourself going in circles or arguing semantics about whether obesity is linked to health problems, and at this point, they start arguing crap like socioeconomics and mental health which is another broad, subjective stance that is difficult to disprove. Once you are arguing semantics and exceptions, you are successfully distracted from the point of the argument and then they just run-out the clock until the debate is over and no one learnt anything.

It's a shitty tactic, but the point is that these are shitty, dishonest people. They use emotional manipulation of the audience to make you try and argue about respect and love and compassion instead of truth. You don't have to fight by their rules, but you are naive to think that you can come prepared with only stats about obesity and health and win. You have to acknowledge, if you live in reality, that you have to appeal to your audience to some degree if you hope to change their minds. If you just scream about links between obesity and diabetes over and over again, it will seem like you aren't addressing their points because they reframed it. That's why I say to be prepared for what the argument will become as well as for what it's meant to be.
